claim: Objects can be recognized based on their intrinsic features, including shape, color, and texture.
source: Objects can be recognized based on their intrinsic features, including shape, color, and texture.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about object recognition.

claim: Object recognition can be highly accurate when objects are seen within their typical scene context, even when intrinsic features are not clearly visible.
source: Interestingly, object recognition can still be highly accurate under these conditions when objects are seen within their typical scene context.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction.

claim: According to parallel processing accounts, context-based object recognition is supported by the parallel processing of object and scene information in separate pathways.
source: According to parallel processing accounts, context-based object recognition is supported by the parallel processing of object and scene information in separate pathways.
evidence: This describes a theoretical account from the literature.

claim: According to feedback accounts, context-based object recognition is supported by feedback from scene-selective to object-selective regions.
source: Alternatively, according to feedback accounts, context-based object recognition is supported by (direct or indirect) feedback from scene-selective to object-selective regions.
evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical account from the literature.

claim: Scene-selective cortex causally and selectively supports context-based object recognition before object-selective cortex does.
source: Here, in three pre-registered transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments, we tested a key prediction of the feedback hypothesis: that scene-selective cortex causally and selectively supports context-based object recognition before object-selective cortex does.
evidence: This is the key hypothesis tested in the experiments, with results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Relative to isolated object recognition, context-based object recognition was selectively and causally supported by OPA at 160–200 ms after onset.
source: Results confirmed our predictions: relative to isolated object recognition, context-based object recognition was selectively and causally supported by OPA at 160–200 ms after onset, followed by LOC at 260–300 ms after onset.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Context-based object recognition was causally supported by LOC at 260–300 ms after onset.
source: Results confirmed our predictions: relative to isolated object recognition, context-based object recognition was selectively and causally supported by OPA at 160–200 ms after onset, followed by LOC at 260–300 ms after onset.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Context-based expectations facilitate object recognition by disambiguating object representations in the visual cortex.
source: These results indicate that context-based expectations facilitate object recognition by disambiguating object representations in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, representing an inference from the data.

claim: Context facilitates the recognition of objects.
source: Decades of behavioral work have shown that context facilitates the recognition of objects (Bar, 2004; Biederman et al., 1982; Oliva and Torralba, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Contextual facilitation is crucial for everyday behavior, allowing us to recognize objects under poor viewing conditions, at a distance, in clutter, and in the periphery where visual resolution is low.
source: This contextual facilitation is crucial for everyday behavior, allowing us to recognize objects under poor viewing conditions (Figure 1), at a distance, in clutter, and in the periphery where visual resolution is low.
evidence: This statement is supported by general knowledge and illustrated by Figure 1.

claim: Isolated object recognition results from the transformation of local, low-level features into view-invariant object representations along the ventral stream.
source: These studies have shown that isolated object recognition results from the transformation of local, low-level features into view-invariant object representations along the ventral stream (DiCarlo et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2009; Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Serre et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Context-based object recognition may be supported by the parallel feedforward processing of local object information in the ventral stream object pathway and global scene processing in a separate scene pathway.
source: One possibility is that context-based object recognition is supported by the parallel feedforward processing of local object information in the ventral stream object pathway and global scene processing in a separate scene pathway (Henderson and Hollingworth, 1999; Park et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes a theoretical possibility supported by citations.

claim: Context-based object recognition may be supported by feedback processing, with scene context providing a prior that is integrated with ambiguous object representations in the visual cortex.
source: Alternatively, context-based object recognition may be supported by feedback processing, with scene context providing a prior that is integrated with ambiguous object representations in the visual cortex (Bar, 2004; Brandman and Peelen, 2017; de Lange et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical possibility supported by citations.

claim: Neuroimaging studies have shown contextual modulation of neural activity in object-selective cortex.
source: Neuroimaging studies have not been able to distinguish between these possibilities because the contextual modulation of neural activity in object-selective cortex (Brandman and Peelen, 2017; Faivre et al., 2019; Gronau et al., 2008; Rémy et al., 2014) could precede but also follow object recognition, for example reflecting post-recognition imagery (Dijkstra et al., 2018; Reddy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging research.

claim: TMS effects are variable across individuals due to individual differences in functional coordinates, skull thickness, and subject-specific gyral folding patterns.
source: Because TMS effects are variable across individuals, for example, due to individual differences in functional coordinates but also skull thickness and subject-specific gyral folding patterns (Opitz et al., 2013), we used a TMS-based assignment procedure to ensure the effectiveness of TMS over each of the three stimulated regions at the individual participant level (van Koningsbruggen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Objects were equally recognizable when presented in isolation (75.8%) and when presented degraded within a scene (76.7%).
source: Across all TMS conditions, objects were equally recognizable when presented in isolation (without degradation; 75.8%) and when presented degraded within a scene (76.7%; main effect of Task: F(1,71)=1.22, p=0.27), showing that scene context can compensate for the loss of object visibility induced by the local degradation (Brandman and Peelen, 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Scene context can compensate for the loss of object visibility induced by local degradation.
source: Across all TMS conditions, objects were equally recognizable when presented in isolation (without degradation; 75.8%) and when presented degraded within a scene (76.7%; main effect of Task: F(1,71)=1.22, p=0.27), showing that scene context can compensate for the loss of object visibility induced by the local degradation (Brandman and Peelen, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, also supported by a citation.

claim: Recognition in the two object recognition tasks was supported by different neural mechanisms in a time-specific manner.
source: Importantly, despite the equal performance, recognition in the two object recognition tasks was supported by different neural mechanisms in a time-specific manner (three-way interaction between Task [intact object recognition, context-based object recognition], Region [OPA, LOC, and EVC], and Time [60–100 ms, 160–200 ms, and 260–300 ms]; F(4,138)=14.37, p<0.001, ηp²=0.294).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: TMS did not significantly affect response time.
source: TMS did not significantly affect response time (RT), with no interactions involving either TMS time or TMS region: Time×Region, F(4,138)=0.163, p=0.957; Task×Region, F(2,69)=0.81, p=0.450; Time×Task, F(2,142)=0.37, p=0.689; Time×Region×Task, F(4,138)=1.153, p=0.334.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Stimulation of scene-selective OPA differentially affected performance in the two tasks.
source: Stimulation of scene-selective OPA differentially affected performance in the two tasks (Figure 3b, left panel; Task×Time interaction F(2,46)=8.21, p<0.001, ηp²=0.263).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Isolated object recognition was not influenced by TMS over OPA.
source: For isolated object recognition, there was no effect of TMS time (F(2,46)=0.07, p=0.935, ηp²=0.003), indicating that isolated object recognition was not influenced by TMS over OPA.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Context-based object recognition was strongly modulated by TMS time over OPA.
source: By contrast, context-based object recognition was strongly modulated by TMS time (F(2,46)=19.54, p<0.001, ηp²=0.459).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: TMS selectively impaired context-based object recognition performance when OPA was stimulated 160–200 ms after scene onset.
source: As predicted, TMS selectively impaired context-based object recognition performance when OPA was stimulated 160–200 ms after scene onset, both relative to earlier stimulation (t(23)=5.39, p<0.001, d=1.099) and relative to later stimulation (t(23)=5.36, p<0.001, d=1.095), with no significant difference between early and late stimulation (t(23)=0.26, p=0.795).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: OPA, a scene-selective region, is causally and selectively involved in context-based object recognition.
source: These results show that OPA, a scene-selective region, is causally and selectively involved in (context-based) object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: OPA stimulation at 160–200 ms after scene onset impaired accuracy in the scene-alone task relative to later stimulation.
source: For the scene-alone task, accuracy was significantly affected by TMS time (F(2,46)=4.77, p=0.013, ηp²=0.172). TMS impaired scene-alone accuracy when OPA was stimulated at 160–200 ms after scene onset relative to later stimulation (t(23)=3.02, p=0.006, d=0.616), though not relative to earlier stimulation (t(23)=1.62, p=0.118).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Stimulation of object-selective LOC differentially affected performance in the two tasks.
source: Stimulation of object-selective LOC differentially affected performance in the two tasks (Figure 3b, middle panel; Task×Time interaction F(2,46)=12.99, p<0.001, ηp²=0.361).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: TMS selectively impaired isolated object recognition performance when LOC was stimulated at 160–200 ms after stimulus onset.
source: As predicted, TMS selectively impaired isolated object recognition performance when LOC was stimulated at 160–200 ms after stimulus onset, both relative to earlier stimulation (t(23)=4.58, p<0.001, d=0.936) and relative to later stimulation (t(23)=5.39, p<0.001, d=1.101), with no significant difference between early and late stimulation (t(23)=−1.17, p=0.255).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Context-based object recognition performance strongly decreased when TMS was applied to LOC at 260–300 ms after stimulus onset.
source: In contrast to the isolated object condition, performance strongly decreased when TMS was applied later in time, at 260–300 ms after stimulus onset, both relative to early stimulation (t(23)=4.01, p<0.001, d=0.818) and relative to middle stimulation (t(23)=2.26, p=0.034, d=0.461).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Context-based object recognition accuracy was moderately reduced when TMS was applied to LOC at 160–200 ms relative to earlier stimulation.
source: Context-based object recognition accuracy was moderately reduced when TMS was applied at 160–200 ms relative to earlier stimulation (t(23)=2.17, p=0.041, d=0.442).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: LOC is causally involved in both isolated object recognition and context-based object recognition at 160–200 ms after stimulus onset.
source: These findings confirm that LOC is causally involved in both isolated object recognition and context-based object recognition at 160–200 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: LOC was causally involved in context-based object recognition at 260–300 ms, confirming the hypothesis that contextual feedback to LOC supports context-based object recognition.
source: Crucially, LOC was causally involved in context-based object recognition at 260–300 ms, confirming our hypothesis that contextual feedback to LOC supports context-based object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: The time of EVC stimulation differentially affected performance in the two tasks.
source: Results showed that the time of EVC stimulation differentially affected performance in the two tasks (Figure 3b, right panel; Task×Time interaction F(2,46)=14.42, p<0.001, ηp²=0.385).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly supported by experimental data with statistical analysis and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: TMS applied early in time to EVC impaired isolated object recognition performance relative to TMS late in time.
source: As predicted, TMS applied early in time impaired recognition performance relative to TMS late in time (t(23)=3.44, p=0.002, d=0.701).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Isolated object recognition was impaired when TMS was applied to EVC at 160–200 ms compared to late stimulation.
source: Interestingly, and contrary to our prediction, isolated object recognition was also impaired when TMS was applied at 160–200 ms compared to late stimulation (t(23)=5.19, p<0.001, d=1.06).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: TMS applied early in time to EVC impaired context-based object recognition performance relative to TMS late in time.
source: As predicted, TMS applied early in time impaired recognition performance relative to TMS late in time (t(23)=5.41, p<0.001, d=1.105).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Context-based object recognition performance was not significantly reduced when TMS was applied to EVC at the middle time window relative to later stimulation.
source: Contrary to our prediction, context-based object recognition performance was not significantly reduced when TMS was applied at the middle time window relative to later stimulation (t(23)=0.99, p=0.334).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: EVC is causally involved in initial visual processing, supporting both isolated object recognition and context-based recognition.
source: These findings confirm that EVC is causally involved in initial visual processing, supporting both isolated object recognition and context-based recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: In the 160–200 ms time window, EVC was causally involved in isolated object recognition but not context-based object recognition.
source: In the 160–200 ms time window, EVC was causally involved in isolated object recognition but not context-based object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Distinct neural mechanisms underlie object recognition based on local features (isolated object recognition) and scene context (context-based object recognition).
source: Altogether, these results reveal distinct neural mechanisms underlying object recognition based on local features (isolated object recognition) and scene context (context-based object recognition).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: During feedforward processing, EVC and object-selective cortex supported both the recognition of objects in scenes and in isolation, while scene-selective cortex was uniquely required for context-based object recognition.
source: During feedforward processing, EVC and object-selective cortex supported both the recognition of objects in scenes and in isolation, while scene-selective cortex was uniquely required for context-based object recognition.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Feedback to EVC causally supported isolated object recognition.
source: Results additionally showed that feedback to EVC causally supported isolated object recognition, while feedback to object-selective cortex causally supported context-based object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Feedback to object-selective cortex causally supported context-based object recognition.
source: Results additionally showed that feedback to EVC causally supported isolated object recognition, while feedback to object-selective cortex causally supported context-based object recognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: There are two routes to object recognition, each characterized by feedforward and feedback processing but involving different brain regions at different time points.
source: These results provide evidence for two routes to object recognition, each characterized by feedforward and feedback processing but involving different brain regions at different time points (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Feedback processing is required for accurate object recognition.
source: The finding that EVC (for isolated object recognition) and LOC (for context-based object recognition) causally supported object recognition well beyond the feedforward sweep suggests that feedback processing is required for accurate object recognition.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Feedback processing in EVC and LOC may be explained under a hierarchical perceptual inference framework, in which a global representation provides a prior that allows for disambiguating relatively more local information.
source: Feedback processing in EVC and LOC may be explained under a common hierarchical perceptual inference framework (Friston, 2005; Haefner et al., 2016; Lee and Mumford, 2003; Rao and Ballard, 1999), in which a global representation provides a prior that allows for disambiguating relatively more local information.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations to prior frameworks.

claim: For context-based object recognition, the scene (represented in OPA) provides a prior for processing the shape of the object (represented in LOC).
source: For context-based object recognition, the scene (represented in OPA) would be the global element, providing a prior for processing the relatively more local shape of the object (represented in LOC).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results within a theoretical framework.

claim: For isolated object recognition, object shape provides a prior for processing the relatively more local inner object features (represented in EVC).
source: For isolated object recognition, object shape would be the global element, providing a prior for processing the relatively more local inner object features (e.g., the eyes of a squirrel; represented in EVC).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results within a theoretical framework.

claim: Feedback based on more global representations serves to disambiguate the representation of more local representations.
source: Feedback based on the more global representations thus serves to disambiguate the representation of more local representations.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results within a theoretical framework.

claim: In the fMRI study by Brandman and Peelen (2017), representations of degraded objects in LOC were facilitated by the presence of scene context.
source: In the fMRI study that used a similar stimulus set as used here (Brandman and Peelen, 2017), representations of degraded objects in LOC were facilitated (relative to degraded objects alone) by the presence of scene context, indicating input from outside of LOC considering that LOC did not represent object information from scenes presented alone.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: The MEG study by Brandman and Peelen (2017) showed two peaks for degraded objects in scenes, one at 160–180 ms and one at 280–300 ms.
source: Furthermore, the corresponding MEG study showed two peaks for degraded objects in scenes, one at 160–180 ms and one at 280–300 ms.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: The later peak (280–300 ms) in the MEG study showed a significant contextual facilitation effect, with better decoding of degraded objects in scenes than degraded objects alone.
source: The later peak showed a significant contextual facilitation effect in the MEG study, with better decoding of degraded objects in scenes than degraded objects alone.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: The current results are best explained by an account in which information from scenes (processed in scene-selective cortex) feeds back to LOC to disambiguate object representations.
source: Taken together with previous findings, the current results are thus best explained by an account in which information from scenes (processed in scene-selective cortex) feeds back to LOC to disambiguate object representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of prior findings.

claim: This mechanism may underlie the behavioral benefits previously observed for object recognition in semantically and syntactically congruent (vs. incongruent) scene context.
source: This mechanism may underlie the behavioral benefits previously observed for object recognition in semantically and syntactically congruent (vs. incongruent) scene context (Biederman et al., 1982; Davenport and Potter, 2004; Munneke et al., 2013; Võ and Wolfe, 2013), as predicted by interactive accounts that propose that contextual facilitation is supported by contextual expectations (Bar, 2004; Davenport and Potter, 2004), with quickly extracted global scene 'gist' priming the representation of candidate objects in the visual cortex (Bar, 2004; Oliva and Torralba, 2007; Torralba, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative connection to prior research findings, supported by citations.

claim: OPA is crucial for extracting global scene information at around 160–200 ms after scene onset.
source: The current TMS results suggest that OPA is crucial for extracting this global scene information at around 160–200 ms after scene onset, and that this information is integrated with local object information in LOC around 100 ms later.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Scene information from OPA is integrated with local object information in LOC around 100 ms after OPA processing (i.e., at 260–300 ms).
source: The current TMS results suggest that OPA is crucial for extracting this global scene information at around 160–200 ms after scene onset, and that this information is integrated with local object information in LOC around 100 ms later.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The current results do not speak to whether OPA-LOC connectivity is direct or indirect.
source: The current results do not speak to whether OPA-LOC connectivity is direct or indirect, for example involving additional brain regions such as other scene-selective regions or the orbitofrontal cortex (Bar, 2004).
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: The study provides causal evidence that context-based expectations facilitate object recognition by disambiguating object representations in the visual cortex.
source: To conclude, the current study provides causal evidence that context-based expectations facilitate object recognition by disambiguating object representations in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion, supported by the experimental data.

claim: Distinct neural mechanisms support object recognition based on local features and global scene context.
source: More generally, results reveal that distinct neural mechanisms support object recognition based on local features and global scene context.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion, supported by the experimental data.

claim: 72 right-handed volunteers participated in the experiment.
source: In total, 72 right-handed volunteers (43 females, mean age ± SD = 23.33 ± 3.59, age range = 18–33) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision took part in the experiment, after participating in a TMS localization experiment (Wischnewski and Peelen, 2021).
evidence: This is a direct report of the participant demographics.

claim: The study procedures were approved by the 'Centrale Commissie voor Mensgebonden Onderzoek (CCMO)' and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study procedures were approved by the 'Centrale Commissie voor Mensgebonden Onderzoek (CCMO)' and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Two TMS pulses separated by 40 ms (25 Hz) were applied to disrupt visual cortex activity.
source: Two TMS pulses (biphasic, wavelength: 280 µs) separated by 40 ms (25 Hz) were applied to disrupt visual cortex activity.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method.

claim: A two-pulse TMS design allows for a broader time window of disruption while maintaining relatively good temporal resolution.
source: Given that latency of visual cortex activation varies across participants, a two-pulse TMS design was chosen since it allows for a broader time window of disruption while maintaining relatively good temporal resolution (O'Shea et al., 2004; Pitcher et al., 2007; Wokke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological justification supported by citations.

claim: The intensity of stimulation was adjusted to 85% of the individual phosphene threshold.
source: The intensity of stimulation was adjusted to 85% of the individual phosphene threshold (PT).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method.

claim: The Talairach coordinates for LOC were 45, –74, 0.
source: The coordinates were 45, –74, 0 for LOC (Pitcher et al., 2009) and 34, –77, 21 for OPA (Julian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method, supported by a citation.

claim: The Talairach coordinates for OPA were 34, –77, 21.
source: The coordinates were 45, –74, 0 for LOC (Pitcher et al., 2009) and 34, –77, 21 for OPA (Julian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method, supported by a citation.

claim: TMS was placed on EVC 2 cm above the inion.
source: TMS was placed on EVC based on its anatomical location, 2 cm above the inion (Koivisto et al., 2010; Pascual-Leone and Walsh, 2001).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental method, supported by citations.

claim: Stimuli consisted of 128 scene photographs with a single object belonging to one of eight categories.
source: Stimuli consisted of 128 scene photographs with a single object belonging to one of the following eight categories: airplane, bird, car, fish, human, mammal, ship, and train.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The scenes spanned a visual angle of 6°×4.5°.
source: The scenes spanned a visual angle of 6°×4.5°.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each stimulus was repeated three times, once for each TMS timing.
source: Each stimulus was repeated three times, once for each TMS timing (60–100 ms, 160–200 ms, and 260–300 ms).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The task resulted in a total of 576 trials.
source: This resulted in a total of 576 trials, which were presented in a random order.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The task was divided into 12 blocks of 48 trials, each lasting approximately 4 min.
source: To avoid fatigue, the task was divided into 12 blocks of 48 trials, each lasting approximately 4 min, with short breaks in between of approximately 1 min.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The total duration of the experiment was approximately 90 min.
source: The total duration of the experiment, including preparation and PT determination, was approximately 90 min.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: At night, the truck is easily recognized by participants when placed in context but not when taken out of context.
source: At night (top panels), the truck is easily recognized by participants when placed in context (left) but not when taken out of context (right).
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, illustrating the contextual facilitation effect.

claim: With sufficient light, the truck is easily recognized also when presented in isolation.
source: With sufficient light (bottom panels), the truck is easily recognized also when presented in isolation.
evidence: This is a description of Figure 1, illustrating object recognition under good viewing conditions.

claim: The local degradation of objects in the context-based object condition strongly reduces object recognition when the degraded objects are presented out of scene context.
source: Note that the local degradation of the objects in the context-based object condition is not clearly visible from these small example images. This degradation strongly reduces object recognition when the degraded objects are presented out of scene context (see Brandman and Peelen, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus properties, supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In previous fMRI and MEG experiments, degraded objects were easy to recognize when presented in scene context (>70% correct in a nine-category task) but hard to recognize when presented alone (37% correct).
source: Behavioral results showed that the degraded objects were easy to recognize when presented in scene context (>70% correct in a nine-category task) but hard to recognize when presented alone (37% correct).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous fMRI experiments, the multivariate representation of the category of degraded objects in LOC was strongly enhanced when the objects were viewed in scene context relative to when they were viewed alone.
source: fMRI results showed that the multivariate representation of the category of the degraded objects in LOC was strongly enhanced when the objects were viewed in scene context relative to when they were viewed alone.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous fMRI experiments, scenes presented alone did not evoke discriminable object category responses in LOC, providing evidence for supra-additive contextual facilitation.
source: Importantly, the corresponding scenes presented alone did not evoke discriminable object category responses in LOC, providing evidence for supra-additive contextual facilitation.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous fMRI experiments, the contextual facilitation of object processing in LOC was correlated with concurrently evoked activity in scene-selective regions.
source: Interestingly, the contextual facilitation of object processing in LOC was correlated with concurrently evoked activity in scene-selective regions, suggesting an interaction between scene- and object-selective regions.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous MEG experiments, information about the category of degraded objects in scenes peaked at 160–180 ms and at 280–300 ms after stimulus onset.
source: MEG results showed that the information about the category of the degraded objects in scenes (derived from multivariate sensor patterns) peaked at two time points: at 160–180 ms and at 280–300 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous MEG experiments, only the later peak (280–300 ms) showed a significant contextual facilitation effect.
source: Crucially, only the later peak showed a significant contextual facilitation effect, with more information about the degraded objects in scenes than the degraded objects alone.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: In previous MEG experiments, at 280–300 ms, scenes alone did not evoke discriminable object category responses.
source: Similar to the LOC results, at this time point, the scenes alone did not evoke discriminable object category responses, such that the contextual facilitation of object processing could not reflect the additive processing of scenes and objects.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research findings.

claim: Previous neuroimaging results indicate that scenes—processed in scene-selective cortex—disambiguate object representations in LOC at around 300 ms after stimulus onset.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that scenes—processed in scene-selective cortex—disambiguate object representations in LOC at around 300 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is an interpretation of prior research findings.
